howItWorks.intro: The calculator multiplies your selected per-class government fee by the number of classes you're filing in, then adds a flat attorney fee if you've chosen to use one. That's the full extent of what a cost calculator can responsibly estimate — it can't tell you whether your mark will clear examination, only what filing it will likely cost up front.

rules.name: Total Cost
rules.formula: Total = (Per Class Fee × Classes) + Attorney Fee
rules.explanation: The USPTO charges its base application fee per class, not per mark, so filing the same mark in two unrelated classes (say, Class 25 for apparel and Class 35 for retail services) doubles the government portion of your bill. The attorney fee, when selected, is added once as a flat amount rather than per class, since most firms quote filing assistance as a single package covering every class in one application.

howItWorks.outro: This is a cost estimate only, not legal advice. It doesn't account for office action responses, opposition proceedings, Statement of Use or extension fees for intent-to-use filings, or state-level trademark registration, all of which can add to the total. Trademark strategy — including the clearance search and which classes to file in — should involve a licensed trademark attorney, since a cost calculator has no way to judge whether your mark is even registrable.

faq.question: What does it cost to file a trademark with the USPTO?
faq.answer: The government filing fee alone runs $250 per class under TEAS Plus or $350 per class under TEAS Standard. A business filing in two classes under TEAS Plus pays $500 to the USPTO; add a $600–$1,500 flat attorney fee and a two-class application with legal help typically lands around $1,100–$2,000 before any office actions come into play.

faq.question: What's the difference between TEAS Plus and TEAS Standard?
faq.answer: TEAS Plus requires you to select your goods/services description straight from the USPTO's pre-approved Trademark ID Manual and costs $250 per class. TEAS Standard lets you write a custom description instead but costs $350 per class and typically asks for more detail up front. Most straightforward applications qualify for TEAS Plus.

faq.question: What's the difference between use-in-commerce and intent-to-use filings?
faq.answer: Use-in-commerce (Section 1(a)) means you're already selling under the mark and submit proof of use with your application. Intent-to-use (Section 1(b)) lets you file before launching, but after the USPTO issues a Notice of Allowance you must file a Statement of Use ($100/class) and pay $125/class for each six-month extension if you're not yet using the mark — up to five extensions, or roughly three years total.

faq.question: Do I need a trademark attorney to file?
faq.answer: No — individuals and most domestic entities can self-file directly through TEAS. But trademark law involves real judgment calls, like whether a mark is merely descriptive or confusingly similar to an existing registration, and a meaningful share of applications draw at least one office action. Many small businesses pay a flat attorney fee of roughly $600–$1,500 specifically to reduce that risk and to get the clearance search and class selection right before filing. This calculator gives a cost estimate, not legal advice.

faq.question: What happens if the USPTO issues an office action?
faq.answer: An office action is the examining attorney's written objection — common reasons include a likelihood-of-confusion refusal, a merely-descriptive refusal, or a rejected specimen of use. You typically have three months (extendable to six, for a fee) to respond. If an attorney handled the original filing, a substantive response often adds $300–$900 in additional fees; if you self-filed, factor that cost in before assuming your filing is finished once the application is submitted.

howWeCalculate.intro: Here's the arithmetic behind each result:
steps: We take your selected filing type — TEAS Plus at $250 per class or TEAS Standard at $350 per class — and multiply it by the number of classes you entered, giving the USPTO Filing Fee.
If you selected 'Use Attorney: Yes,' a flat attorney fee is added on top of the government fee to represent typical flat-fee filing assistance for a straightforward, single-mark application.
The USPTO Filing Fee and Attorney Fee are added together to produce the Total Cost shown in the results.
The breakdown is shown as separate line items so you can see how much of your total is a fixed government charge versus a legal fee you could negotiate, reduce, or skip.
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: These figures reflect the USPTO's published per-class fee structure and typical flat-fee attorney pricing for a straightforward filing; they don't include office action response fees, Statement of Use or extension fees for intent-to-use applications, or the cost of a clearance search, monitoring, or international filing under the Madrid Protocol. Confirm current USPTO fees at uspto.gov before filing, and treat this tool as a cost estimate, not legal advice.
